content: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the targets and indicators of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Thirteenth General Programme of Work emphasize achieving universal health coverage. International human rights law obligates WHO Member States to ensure that women and adolescent girls survive pregnancy and childbirth, as part of their sexual and reproductive health rights and their right to live a life of dignity. The WHO envisions a world where every pregnant woman and newborn receives high-quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. Evidence shows that effective interventions exist at reasonable costs to prevent or treat nearly all life-threatening maternal complications. Approximately two-thirds of the global maternal and neonatal disease burden could be alleviated by optimally adapting and implementing existing research findings. To deliver high-quality care, healthcare providers at all levels of maternal healthcare services, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, must have access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures. Additionally, healthcare providers, managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders require up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, optimize care quality, and improve healthcare outcomes. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are a significant cause of severe morbidity, long-term disability, and death among mothers and their babies. Globally, these disorders account for approximately 14% of all maternal deaths. Among these, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are major contributors to maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity. Most deaths due to pre-eclampsia and eclampsia could be prevented with timely and effective care for women presenting with these complications. Efforts to prevent and reduce morbidity and mortality associated with pre-eclampsia and eclampsia could address profound global inequities in maternal health. In 2011, WHO published 22 recommendations for the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, including a recommendation on calcium supplementation during pregnancy. These recommendations were developed using WHO guideline development standards, which included synthesizing available research evidence, applying the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology, and formulating recommendations through a panel of international experts. In 2016, the WHO guideline panel on antenatal care recommendations for a positive pregnancy experience reviewed updated evidence and revised the calcium supplementation recommendation. While consistent with the 2011 recommendation, additional remarks and implementation considerations were added, particularly regarding the integration of the recommendation into the WHO 2016 antenatal care package. WHO has established a novel process for prioritizing and updating maternal and perinatal health recommendations. An Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) oversees the systematic prioritization of recommendations most urgently needing updates. Recommendations are prioritized based on changes or new uncertainties in the evidence base regarding benefits, harms, values, acceptability, feasibility, equity, resource use, cost-effectiveness, or implementation factors. The Executive GSG identified updating the WHO recommendation on calcium supplementation during pregnancy as a high priority in response to new, potentially important evidence. The primary goal of this recommendation is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for pregnant women, particularly those related to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and associated complications. This recommendation provides a foundation for the sustainable global implementation of calcium supplementation during pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia and its complications. The primary audience for this recommendation includes healthcare professionals responsible for developing national and local health guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, as well as those directly providing care to women during labor and childbirth. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, managers of maternal and child health programs, and relevant staff in ministries of health across all settings. The recommendation was framed using the Population (P), Intervention (I), Comparison (C), Outcome (O) (PICO) format. The key questions addressed were: In pregnant women, does calcium supplementation compared to placebo or no calcium supplementation improve maternal and perinatal outcomes, including the onset of pre-eclampsia? If so, in what populations or contexts is calcium supplementation most beneficial? What dosing regimen of calcium supplementation is most effective? The population affected by this recommendation includes all pregnant women, particularly those at higher risk of gestational hypertensive disorders, in low-, middle-, or high-income settings, and those living in areas with low dietary calcium intake. The recommendation was developed using standardized operating procedures in accordance with the WHO handbook for guideline development. The process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing evidence, formulating the recommendation, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating. In 2017, the WHO recommendation on calcium supplementation during pregnancy was identified as a high priority for updating due to new evidence. Six main groups were involved in this process, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group, WHO Steering Group, Guideline Development Group, External Review Group, systematic review team, and external partners and observers. The Executive GSG, an independent panel of 14 external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions, advised WHO on prioritizing new and existing questions in maternal and perinatal health for recommendation development or updating. The WHO Steering Group, comprising WHO staff from relevant departments, managed the updating process, drafted key recommendation questions, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, and supervised evidence synthesis and retrieval. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included 16 external experts and stakeholders selected for their expertise in research, guideline development methods, clinical policy, and programs related to pre-eclampsia and eclampsia prevention and treatment. The GDG appraised the evidence, advised on its interpretation, formulated the final recommendation, and reached unanimous consensus on the recommendation in the final document. An External Review Group, comprising eight technical experts, reviewed the final document for factual errors, clarity of language, contextual issues, and implementation implications. They ensured that decision-making processes incorporated contextual values and preferences of potential users of the recommendations, including healthcare professionals and policymakers. A Cochrane systematic review on calcium supplementation during pregnancy was updated and served as the primary source of evidence for this recommendation. Randomized controlled trials relevant to the key question were screened, and data on relevant outcomes and comparisons were entered into Review Manager (RevMan) software. The evidence was critically appraised using the GRADE methodology, and evidence profiles were prepared for comparisons of interest. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, with ratings of ‘high,’ ‘moderate,’ ‘low,’ or ‘very low’ based on established criteria. Factors influencing the final rating included study design limitations, inconsistency of results, and indirectness of evidence.
